whyWrongByChoice.E: Retroperitoneal varices are internal collaterals and do not produce the visible periumbilical pattern.

questions.stem: A physiology instructor asks why pain from an inflamed abdominal viscus is frequently perceived at a distant body-wall location. Which mechanism best explains referred pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visceral afferents enter the spinal cord at the same levels as somatic afferents, and the brain misattributes the signal to the somatic dermatome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Visceral afferents enter the spinal cord through the ventral roots

choices.label: C
choices.text: Visceral afferents travel entirely independently of autonomic pathways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visceral afferents are precisely localized to individual organs without any overlap

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic afferents synapse directly on postganglionic sympathetic neurons

explanation.summary: Referred pain arises because visceral and somatic afferents converge at the same spinal cord levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both visceral and somatic afferents enter the cord through the dorsal roots at shared spinal levels; the CNS cannot distinguish the source, so visceral pain is felt in the corresponding somatic dermatome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Afferent (sensory) fibers enter through the dorsal roots, not the ventral (motor) roots.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Visceral afferents actually travel alongside autonomic fibers, which is part of the pathway that enables referral.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Visceral afferents are poorly localized with substantial convergence, which is precisely why pain is referred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic afferents are sensory and do not synapse on postganglionic sympathetic neurons; this does not explain referred pain.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma has intractable visceral upper abdominal pain that is poorly controlled with opioids. A procedure that permanently destroys the plexus surrounding the celiac trunk with injected alcohol is planned. What is this procedure?

explanation.summary: Celiac plexus neurolysis with alcohol relieves intractable visceral foregut pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The celiac plexus transmits visceral afferent pain from foregut structures including the pancreas; injecting alcohol permanently destroys the plexus, providing durable relief in pancreatic cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vagotomy severs parasympathetic (efferent) vagal fibers to reduce acid secretion; it is not used for pancreatic cancer pain neurolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pelvic splanchnic blocks target hindgut/pelvic parasympathetics, not foregut visceral pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L1-L2 sympathectomy is not the standard procedure for foregut visceral pain; the celiac plexus is the target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A TAP block anesthetizes the anterior abdominal wall (somatic), not visceral foregut afferents.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with weight loss and early satiety is found to have gastric adenocarcinoma. On exam, a firm, enlarged lymph node is palpated just above the left clavicle. Enlargement of which lymph node does this represent?

explanation.summary: A left supraclavicular (Virchow) node enlarged by abdominal malignancy is the Troisier sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Virchow node sits near the thoracic duct termination at the left subclavian vein; metastatic abdominal cancer (e.g., gastric) can seed it, producing a palpable left supraclavicular node (Troisier sign).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The right supraclavicular node drains the right lymphatic duct territory (right thorax/upper body), not the abdomen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Axillary nodes drain the upper limb and breast, not gastric lymphatics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and perineum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A periumbilical node (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) is also a metastatic sign, but the described location is the left supraclavicular Virchow node.

questions.stem: During bowel resection, a surgeon distinguishes jejunum from ileum by inspecting the mesenteric vasculature. Which vascular feature is characteristic of the jejunum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Short vasa recta with numerous arterial arcades

choices.label: B
choices.text: Short vasa recta with a single arterial arcade

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long vasa recta with few arterial arcades

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct arterial supply from the IMA

explanation.summary: The jejunum has long vasa recta and few arterial arcades.
explanation.whyCorrect: The jejunum is characterized by long vasa recta and fewer, larger arcades, providing greater perfusion; the ileum has short vasa recta and more numerous arcades.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Short vasa recta with numerous arcades describes the ileum, not the jejunum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A single arcade with short vasa recta does not describe the jejunum's long vasa recta pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both jejunum and ileum have vasa recta; they are not absent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both jejunum and ileum are midgut and supplied by the SMA, not the IMA.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old presents with abdominal pain that began around the umbilicus and later migrated to the right lower quadrant, with fever and leukocytosis. Which mechanism best explains why the EARLY pain was localized to the periumbilical region?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visceral referred pain from the midgut appendix enters the cord at the T10 level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Somatic afferents from the parietal peritoneum were directly stimulated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Foregut afferents referred pain to the periumbilical dermatome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phrenic nerve irritation referred pain to the umbilicus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hindgut afferents entering at T12-L2 caused periumbilical pain

explanation.summary: Early appendicitis pain is periumbilical because it is midgut visceral referred pain at T10.
explanation.whyCorrect: The appendix is a midgut structure; its visceral afferents enter the cord around T10, so early inflammation produces diffuse periumbilical (T10 dermatome) referred pain before the parietal peritoneum is involved.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Parietal peritoneal (somatic) stimulation causes the LATER, sharply localized RLQ pain, not the early periumbilical pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foregut afferents (T5-T9) refer to the epigastrium, not the umbilicus, and the appendix is not foregut.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) irritation refers pain to the shoulder, not the umbilicus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hindgut afferents (T12-L2) refer to the suprapubic region; the appendix is midgut, not hindgut.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with cirrhosis has hematemesis from bleeding submucosal veins of the distal esophagus. Elevated portal pressure is transmitted to the esophageal veins primarily through which vein?

explanation.summary: Esophageal varices form via portal pressure transmitted through the left gastric (coronary) vein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The left gastric vein drains into the portal vein and anastomoses with esophageal veins of the azygos system; portal hypertension backs up into these submucosal esophageal veins, producing varices that can bleed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The splenic vein contributes to portal pressure but does not directly connect to the distal esophageal veins responsible for varices.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The SMV drains the midgut and is not the direct route to esophageal varices.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The IMV drains the hindgut and is associated with rectal, not esophageal, varices.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The paraumbilical vein is the route for caput medusae, not esophageal varices.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is reviewing autonomic effects on the gut. Increased sympathetic activity to the GI tract produces which set of effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased motility, increased secretion, increased blood flow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased motility, decreased secretion, increased blood flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased motility, decreased secretion, decreased blood flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased motility, increased secretion, decreased blood flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: No effect on motility, increased blood flow, increased secretion

explanation.summary: Sympathetic activation decreases GI motility, secretion, and blood flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sympathetic ('fight or flight') input opposes the parasympathetic 'rest and digest' state, reducing GI motility, secretion, and mucosal blood flow while promoting sphincter contraction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased motility, secretion, and blood flow describe parasympathetic, not sympathetic, effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This mixes increased motility/blood flow (parasympathetic-like) with decreased secretion, which is inconsistent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sympathetic activity decreases, not increases, secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sympathetic input decreases blood flow and secretion and does reduce motility; it is not neutral.

questions.stem: An examiner asks a student to name a primary branch of the celiac trunk. Which of the following is a direct branch of the celiac trunk?

explanation.summary: The celiac trunk gives rise to the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.
explanation.whyCorrect: The splenic artery is one of the three primary branches of the celiac trunk (along with the left gastric and common hepatic arteries), supplying the spleen, pancreas, and parts of the stomach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The SMA is a separate unpaired aortic branch, not a branch of the celiac trunk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The IMA is a separate unpaired aortic branch supplying the hindgut.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ileocolic artery is a branch of the SMA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The middle colic artery is a branch of the SMA.

questions.stem: An interventional radiologist notes that cardioemboli travel down the aorta and preferentially enter one mesenteric artery. Which combination of anatomic features best explains why the SMA is the most common site of embolic lodgment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Small diameter, low flow, and a perpendicular takeoff angle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Large diameter, low flow, and a steep downward takeoff angle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Small diameter, high flow, and a horizontal takeoff angle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large diameter, high flow, and a shallow (oblique) takeoff angle from the aorta

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absence of collateral circulation and a right-angle takeoff

explanation.summary: The SMA's large caliber, high flow, and shallow takeoff angle make it the favored embolic site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the SMA branches from the aorta at a shallow oblique angle with a large diameter and high blood flow, emboli carried by the aortic stream easily enter and lodge in it, causing acute mesenteric ischemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The SMA is large with high flow, not small with low flow, and its angle is oblique, not perpendicular.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The SMA has high flow, not low flow, and a shallow rather than steep downward angle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The SMA is large-caliber, not small, though it does have high flow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mesenteric circulation has collateral pathways (e.g., marginal artery), and the SMA takeoff is oblique, not a right angle.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with sudden severe abdominal and back pain. He is pale and diaphoretic with a blood pressure of 86/52 mmHg, heart rate 118/min, and a tender pulsatile midline mass. He remains alive when he reaches the operating room hours later. Which anatomic feature best explains why he survived long enough to reach surgery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The aorta is retroperitoneal, and closed fascial compartments there tamponaded the hemorrhage

choices.label: B
choices.text: The greater omentum wrapped around the aorta and sealed the leak

choices.label: C
choices.text: The aorta is intraperitoneal, allowing blood to disperse harmlessly across serosal surfaces

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood drained into the rectovesical pouch and was reabsorbed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hepatorenal recess absorbed the blood before it reached the peritoneal cavity

explanation.summary: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is temporarily survivable when it bleeds into the retroperitoneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aorta is a retroperitoneal structure. The closed fascial compartments of the retroperitoneum can tamponade the bleed, containing it long enough for the patient to reach definitive repair.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The omentum does not seal a high-pressure aortic rupture; containment comes from retroperitoneal fascial planes, not omental adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The aorta is retroperitoneal, not intraperitoneal, and free intraperitoneal aortic rupture is immediately lethal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Massive arterial hemorrhage is not reabsorbed from a pelvic pouch; this cannot explain survival.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hepatorenal recess is a potential space for passive fluid collection in supine patients, not a compartment that stops arterial bleeding.

questions.stem: During a Whipple procedure, a surgeon clamps the free edge of the lesser omentum (Pringle maneuver) to control bleeding from the liver. Which set of structures is being compressed within this ligament?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Splenic artery, splenic vein, and pancreatic duct

choices.label: B
choices.text: Portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and bile duct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inferior vena cava, right hepatic vein, and cystic duct

choices.label: D
choices.text: Superior mesenteric artery, superior mesenteric vein, and left gastric artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein

explanation.summary: The hepatoduodenal ligament, the free edge of the lesser omentum, carries the portal triad.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hepatoduodenal ligament contains the portal triad: the portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and bile duct. Compressing it (Pringle maneuver) occludes hepatic inflow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These lie along the pancreas and splenic hilum, not within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The IVC lies posterior to the omental foramen, not within the ligament; the hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The SMA and SMV lie in the root of the mesentery behind the pancreas, not in the lesser omentum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are posterior mediastinal/retroperitoneal structures unrelated to the lesser omentum.

questions.stem: A physiologist compares the two esophageal sphincters. The upper esophageal sphincter can be voluntarily influenced and is composed of skeletal muscle, whereas the sphincter at the gastroesophageal junction maintains tone without voluntary control. What is the muscular composition of this lower sphincter?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Striated muscle continuous with the diaphragm

explanation.summary: The lower esophageal sphincter is a specialization of smooth muscle, unlike the skeletal UES.
explanation.whyCorrect: The LES is formed by a thickened region of inner circular smooth muscle at the distal esophagus that stays tonically contracted to prevent reflux.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cricopharyngeus is the upper esophageal sphincter (skeletal muscle), not the LES.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The crural diaphragm acts as an external augmenting sphincter but is not the LES itself, and the LES is smooth muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The longitudinal esophageal muscle is not the sphincter, and the distal esophageal muscle is smooth, not skeletal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The oblique layer is gastric and is smooth muscle, not the esophageal sphincter.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with Crohn disease undergoes resection of a strictured terminal ileum. One year later she develops macrocytic anemia and paresthesias despite a normal diet. Loss of which absorptive function of the resected segment best explains her findings?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts

explanation.summary: The terminal ileum is the dedicated site for vitamin B12 and bile salt absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 (bound to intrinsic factor) and bile salts are absorbed primarily in the terminal ileum, so terminal ileal resection produces B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate is absorbed mainly in the proximal jejunum, not the terminal ileum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron is absorbed chiefly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium is absorbed predominantly in the duodenum (vitamin D dependent).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most water is absorbed throughout the jejunum and ileum, but that would not selectively cause macrocytic anemia and neuropathy.

questions.stem: An embryology lecture describes organs that initially develop suspended by a dorsal mesentery but later become fixed to the posterior body wall as their mesentery fuses with the parietal peritoneum. Which pair of organs is the best example of this developmental fate?

explanation.summary: Secondarily retroperitoneal organs begin with a mesentery, then fuse to the posterior wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pancreas and most of the duodenum are classic secondarily retroperitoneal structures: they develop with a mesentery and later fuse to the posterior wall, losing mobility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stomach and spleen remain intraperitoneal and mobile.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The transverse and sigmoid colon retain true mesenteries (mesocolon) and remain intraperitoneal; it is the ascending and descending colon that become secondarily retroperitoneal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver and gallbladder are intraperitoneal (the gallbladder lies on the liver's visceral surface).
whyWrongByChoice.D: The jejunum and appendix are intraperitoneal with a mesentery/mesoappendix.

questions.stem: A supine trauma patient undergoes a FAST ultrasound. The sonographer looks for free intraperitoneal blood in the most dependent recess of the right upper quadrant, located between the liver and the right kidney. Which space is being examined?

explanation.summary: Morison's pouch is the dependent RUQ space where fluid collects in supine patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) lies between the liver and right kidney and is the most dependent space of the upper peritoneal cavity when supine, making it a key FAST window.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The pouch of Douglas is the most dependent pelvic space in females, not the RUQ space between liver and kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and does not communicate freely with the general peritoneal cavity to collect free fluid on FAST.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The left subphrenic space is under the left hemidiaphragm, not between the liver and right kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The paracolic gutter runs alongside the colon and is not the space between liver and right kidney.

questions.stem: During surgery a resident passes a finger through a natural opening posterior to the free edge of the lesser omentum, entering a space behind the stomach. Through which structure has the finger passed, and what does it connect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The falciform ligament, connecting the liver to the anterior abdominal wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: The epiploic (omental) foramen, connecting the greater and lesser sacs

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rectouterine pouch, connecting the pelvis to the paracolic gutter

choices.label: D
choices.text: The esophageal hiatus, connecting the thorax and abdomen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mesoappendix, connecting the appendix to the ileum

explanation.summary: The epiploic foramen is the passage between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The epiploic (omental) foramen is bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of the lesser omentum) and connects the greater sac with the lesser sac behind the stomach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The falciform ligament is an anterior peritoneal fold to the abdominal wall and is not a foramen between sacs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rectouterine pouch is a pelvic recess, not a communication between the greater and lesser sacs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The esophageal hiatus transmits the esophagus through the diaphragm, not a peritoneal sac connection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mesoappendix suspends the appendix and is unrelated to the lesser sac.

questions.stem: On a CT scan, a peritoneal fold is seen running along the anterior surface of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall. Within its free inferior edge lies a fibrous cord that is a remnant of a fetal vessel. Which fold and remnant are described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coronary ligament containing the ligamentum venosum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gastrosplenic ligament containing the short gastric vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Falciform ligament containing the ligamentum teres

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatogastric ligament containing the left gastric artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gastrocolic ligament containing the gastroepiploic vessels

explanation.summary: The falciform ligament carries the ligamentum teres, the obliterated fetal umbilical vein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The falciform ligament anchors the liver to the anterior abdominal wall, and its free edge contains the ligamentum teres, a remnant of the fetal (left) umbilical vein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ligamentum venosum is a remnant of the ductus venosus and lies in a fissure on the liver, not in the falciform ligament.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric vessels but does not attach the liver to the anterior wall or contain the ligamentum teres.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hepatogastric ligament carries the left gastric vessels and is part of the lesser omentum, not the anterior fold containing the ligamentum teres.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The gastrocolic ligament is part of the greater omentum and does not carry the ligamentum teres.

questions.stem: A patient with autoimmune atrophic gastritis has selective destruction of the parietal cells located in a particular gastric region, leading to loss of intrinsic factor and gastric acid. In which region of the stomach are the cells producing HCl, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen predominantly found?

explanation.summary: HCl, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen come from the acid-secreting body and fundus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The body and fundus contain parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen). Their loss in atrophic gastritis causes achlorhydria and B12 malabsorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cardia mainly secretes mucus and lies at the gastroesophageal junction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The antrum produces gastrin (G cells) and somatostatin (D cells), not HCl or intrinsic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pylorus is a muscular sphincter region and is not the main source of these secretions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pyloric canal is part of the distal gastric outlet and does not produce intrinsic factor or acid.

questions.stem: During ERCP, an endoscopist advances the scope into the duodenum and cannulates the major duodenal papilla to inject contrast into the biliary and pancreatic ducts. In which part of the duodenum is this papilla located?

explanation.summary: The major duodenal papilla lies in the second (descending) part of the duodenum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The second (descending) part of the duodenum receives bile and pancreatic secretions through the major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The first part (superior/bulb) is proximal to the papilla and is a common ulcer site, not where the ducts open.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The fourth part ascends to the duodenojejunal flexure and does not contain the papilla.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The duodenal bulb is the initial superior segment, not the location of the major papilla.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The third (horizontal) part crosses at L3 anterior to the aorta but is distal to the papilla.

questions.stem: A surgeon inspects two loops of small bowel to decide which is jejunum. Compared with the ileum, which combination of features identifies the jejunum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Larger diameter, thicker walls, longer vasa recta, and fewer arterial arcades

choices.label: B
choices.text: Smaller diameter, thinner walls, shorter vasa recta, and more arterial arcades

choices.label: C
choices.text: More mesenteric fat, abundant Peyer patches, and short vasa recta

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thinner walls, more arcades, and primary site of vitamin B12 absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Larger diameter, teniae coli, and haustra

explanation.summary: The jejunum has a larger caliber, thicker wall, longer vasa recta, and fewer arcades than the ileum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The jejunum characteristically has a larger diameter, thicker walls, longer vasa recta, and fewer arterial arcades, with less mesenteric fat than the ileum.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These are ileal features (thinner walls, shorter vasa recta, more arcades).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Abundant Peyer patches, more mesenteric fat, and short vasa recta describe the ileum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thinner walls, more arcades, and B12 absorption are ileal characteristics.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teniae coli and haustra are features of the large intestine, not the jejunum.

questions.stem: A medical student examines a bowel specimen showing three distinct longitudinal bands of smooth muscle running along its outer surface, with sacculations between them. These bands are a defining feature of which segment of the GI tract?

explanation.summary: Teniae coli are the three longitudinal muscle bands unique to the colon.
explanation.whyCorrect: The colon is identified by teniae coli (three longitudinal smooth-muscle bands), along with haustra and omental appendices, distinguishing it from small bowel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The jejunum has a continuous longitudinal muscle layer and plicae circulares, not teniae coli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The duodenum lacks teniae coli.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The esophagus has continuous inner circular and outer longitudinal layers, not teniae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ileum, like other small bowel, has a complete longitudinal layer, not three bands.

questions.stem: A patient has a small tumor in the anal canal just distal to the dentate (pectinate) line. Compared with a lesion just proximal to this line, the distal lesion is more likely to cause sharp, well-localized pain. Which statement best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The proximal portion drains to superficial inguinal nodes and is somatically innervated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both portions are entirely under voluntary somatic control

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distal portion is somatically innervated, whereas the proximal portion has autonomic (visceral) innervation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distal portion is lined by columnar epithelium with visceral innervation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The dentate line marks the junction of the sigmoid colon and rectum

explanation.summary: The dentate line separates autonomically innervated proximal canal from somatically innervated distal canal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Above the dentate line the canal is under autonomic (visceral) control and is relatively insensitive to pain; below it the canal has somatic innervation (inferior rectal nerve), making distal lesions sharply painful.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The proximal (above-line) portion is autonomically innervated and drains to internal iliac nodes; it is the distal portion that drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only the distal third is under somatic control; the proximal two-thirds is autonomic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Below the dentate line the lining is stratified squamous epithelium with somatic innervation, not columnar/visceral.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The dentate line is within the anal canal, not the rectosigmoid junction.

questions.stem: A woman with pelvic inflammatory disease develops a pelvic abscess. The clinician expects pus to collect in the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in a supine female. Which space is this?

explanation.summary: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the lowest peritoneal space in females.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas), between the uterus and rectum, is the most dependent point of the female peritoneal cavity and a common site for fluid or abscess accumulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vesicouterine pouch (between bladder and uterus) is shallower and more anterior, not the most dependent point.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hepatorenal recess is the dependent space of the upper abdomen when supine, not the pelvis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The right subphrenic space is high under the diaphragm, not dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rectovesical pouch is the corresponding pouch in males, who lack a uterus.

questions.stem: An elderly patient with a stroke develops difficulty initiating swallowing and food catching in the throat. Videofluoroscopy shows failure of relaxation of the skeletal-muscle upper esophageal sphincter. Which muscle forms this sphincter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inner circular smooth muscle of the distal esophagus

explanation.summary: The upper esophageal sphincter is the cricopharyngeus, a skeletal muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: The UES is formed by the cricopharyngeus, a skeletal muscle that stays tonically contracted and relaxes during swallowing; its dysfunction causes oropharyngeal dysphagia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inner circular smooth muscle forms the lower esophageal sphincter, not the UES.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The right crus of the diaphragm augments the LES externally at the hiatus, not the UES.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The thyropharyngeus is the upper part of the inferior constrictor; the cricopharyngeus (its lower fibers) specifically forms the UES.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oblique gastric layer is part of the stomach wall, unrelated to the UES.

questions.stem: An upright chest radiograph shows a gastric air bubble in the most superior part of the stomach, lying just beneath the left hemidiaphragm and above the level of the gastroesophageal junction. Which gastric region does this air bubble occupy?

explanation.summary: The fundus is the most superior gastric region and holds the gastric gas bubble.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fundus is the dome-shaped superior portion of the stomach lying above the gastroesophageal junction; swallowed air rises here, producing the gastric bubble on upright imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The antrum is the distal region leading to the pylorus, inferior and to the right.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pylorus is the muscular outlet at the gastroduodenal junction, not the superior gas-filled dome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The body is the central region below the fundus, not the most superior part.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The cardia surrounds the GEJ but is not the highest point where gas collects.

questions.stem: A neonate with bilious vomiting undergoes an upper GI series to evaluate for intestinal malrotation. The radiologist looks for the normal position of the duodenojejunal flexure, an important landmark for this diagnosis. This flexure normally marks the transition to which intraperitoneal segment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transition from stomach to duodenum at the pylorus

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transition from retroperitoneal duodenum to intraperitoneal jejunum

choices.label: C
choices.text: The transition from ileum to cecum at the ileocecal valve

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transition from ascending to transverse colon

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transition from sigmoid colon to rectum

explanation.summary: The duodenojejunal flexure marks where the fixed duodenum becomes the mobile jejunum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The duodenojejunal flexure marks the transition from the secondarily retroperitoneal duodenum to the intraperitoneal jejunum. Its position (relative to the ligament of Treitz) is the key landmark for diagnosing malrotation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gastroduodenal transition is the pylorus, not the duodenojejunal flexure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ileocecal valve marks the ileum-to-cecum transition, a different landmark.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hepatic flexure marks the ascending-to-transverse colon transition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rectosigmoid junction is distal and unrelated to the duodenojejunal flexure.

questions.stem: A patient with obstructed defecation is counseled that adopting a squatting posture eases stool passage. This works because a sling-like muscle around the anorectal junction relaxes, changing an angle. Which muscle relaxes and what is the effect on the anorectal angle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Internal anal sphincter contracts, narrowing the angle

choices.label: B
choices.text: External anal sphincter contracts, closing the canal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Puborectalis relaxes, widening (straightening) the anorectal angle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Puborectalis contracts, sharpening the anorectal angle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Levator ani contracts, elevating the pelvic floor to hold stool

explanation.summary: Relaxation of the puborectalis straightens the anorectal angle to allow defecation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The puborectalis forms a sling that maintains the acute anorectal angle at rest. During defecation it relaxes, widening (straightening) the angle so stool can pass; squatting enhances this.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Internal anal sphincter contraction maintains continence and would impede, not ease, defecation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: External anal sphincter contraction closes the canal, opposing defecation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Puborectalis contraction sharpens the angle and maintains continence, the opposite of what aids defecation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Levator ani contraction that elevates the floor supports continence rather than easing passage.

questions.stem: A physiologist reviews where fluid is reclaimed along the GI tract. Of the roughly 9 liters of fluid entering the gut daily, which statement correctly identifies where the majority of water is absorbed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stomach absorbs most of the water before chyme enters the duodenum

choices.label: B
choices.text: The large intestine absorbs about 90% of the water

choices.label: C
choices.text: The esophagus absorbs the bulk of ingested water during transit

choices.label: D
choices.text: The small intestine (jejunum and ileum) absorbs about 90% of the water

choices.label: E
choices.text: Water absorption is distributed evenly across all GI segments

explanation.summary: About 90% of GI water is absorbed in the small intestine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The jejunum and ileum absorb roughly 90% of the water in the GI tract; the large intestine reclaims the remainder to form solid stool.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stomach absorbs very little water; its role is mechanical and chemical digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The large intestine absorbs only the residual ~10% of water, not the majority.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The esophagus is a conduit and does not absorb significant water.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absorption is not even; it is concentrated in the small intestine.

questions.stem: A surgeon drains a pelvic abscess in a male patient by locating the single peritoneal pouch present in the male pelvis, the most dependent peritoneal recess in males. Which pouch is this?

explanation.summary: In males the only peritoneal pouch is the rectovesical pouch, the most dependent male pelvic recess.
explanation.whyCorrect: Males have a single peritoneal pouch, the rectovesical pouch, located between the rectum and bladder; it is the most dependent peritoneal space in the male pelvis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rectouterine pouch requires a uterus and is present only in females.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vesicouterine pouch is also a female-only pouch (between bladder and uterus).
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hepatorenal recess is an upper-abdominal space, not a pelvic pouch.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The subphrenic recess is high under the diaphragm, not a dependent pelvic pouch.

questions.stem: During week 4 of development, lateral folding of the trilaminar embryo creates a single midline primitive gut tube. The innermost lining (epithelium) of this tube is derived from which embryonic germ layer or tissue?

explanation.summary: The gut tube epithelium comes from endoderm; the rest of the wall comes from splanchnic mesoderm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lining (epithelium) of the GI tract tube is derived from endoderm, which becomes surrounded by splanchnic mesoderm during lateral folding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ectoderm forms the epidermis and nervous system, not the gut epithelium (except the extreme oral and anal ends from stomodeum/proctodeum).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall on the opposite side of the coelom, not the gut lining.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neural crest contributes enteric ganglia (neurons), not the epithelial lining.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splanchnic mesoderm forms the muscular and connective wall of the tube, not its epithelial lining.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked which artery supplies the foregut and its derivatives (esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas). Which artery is correct?

explanation.summary: Foregut derivatives are supplied by the celiac artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The foregut is vascularized by the celiac artery, the midgut by the SMA, and the hindgut by the IMA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, not the foregut.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The splenic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk, not the primary named foregut vessel asked for.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The left gastric artery is a celiac branch, not the whole foregut supply.

questions.stem: Which of the following adult structures is derived from the midgut?

explanation.summary: The jejunum is a midgut derivative.
explanation.whyCorrect: The midgut becomes the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stomach is a foregut derivative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The liver is a foregut derivative arising from the hepatic diverticulum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The gallbladder is a foregut derivative from the caudal hepatic diverticulum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sigmoid colon is a hindgut derivative.

questions.stem: The hindgut gives rise to the distal third of the transverse colon, the descending and sigmoid colon, the rectum, and the proximal anus. Which artery supplies these hindgut derivatives?

explanation.summary: The hindgut is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hindgut derivatives are vascularized by the IMA, mirroring the celiac (foregut) and SMA (midgut) pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The celiac artery supplies the foregut.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The internal iliac artery supplies the lower rectum and pelvis but is not the primary embryologic hindgut artery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The middle colic artery is an SMA branch supplying the midgut portion of the transverse colon.

questions.stem: In the adult abdomen, the embryonic coelom (primitive body cavity) that separates the somatic and splanchnic mesoderm layers develops into which cavity?

explanation.summary: The coelom becomes the peritoneal cavity in the abdomen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The coelom is the primitive body cavity between somatic and splanchnic mesoderm; in the abdomen it becomes the peritoneal cavity surrounding the intraperitoneal organs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The pleural cavity forms in the thorax, not from the abdominal coelom.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart in the thorax.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The amniotic cavity is an extraembryonic fluid-filled sac, not derived from the intraembryonic coelom.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The omental bursa is only a subdivision created by stomach rotation, not the entire peritoneal cavity.

questions.stem: An anatomist notes that one segment of bowel receives blood from branches of both the celiac artery and the superior mesenteric artery because it straddles a developmental junction. Which structure is this?

explanation.summary: The duodenum spans the foregut-midgut junction and has dual arterial supply.
explanation.whyCorrect: The proximal duodenum is foregut (celiac supply) and the distal duodenum is midgut (SMA supply); the junction lies just distal to the common bile duct entrance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The esophagus is entirely foregut, supplied by the celiac and thoracic branches, not dually with the SMA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stomach is entirely foregut, celiac-supplied.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The descending colon is entirely hindgut, IMA-supplied.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cecum is entirely midgut, SMA-supplied.

questions.stem: A term newborn does well on day 1, then develops abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. An abdominal x-ray shows dilated proximal small bowel loops with a distal narrowing consistent with jejunal stenosis. This narrowing is best explained by which developmental error?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete failure of endodermal cell removal during recanalization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of the midgut loop to herniate into the umbilicus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incomplete removal of luminal cells during recanalization

explanation.summary: Stenosis (narrowing) results from incomplete cell removal during recanalization.
explanation.whyCorrect: During recanalization the endoderm fills the lumen and is then removed; incomplete removal leaves a narrowed (stenotic) lumen, whereas complete failure causes atresia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete failure of cell removal produces atresia (full obstruction), not the partial narrowing described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A persistent vitelline duct causes Meckel diverticulum or fistula, not jejunal stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed herniation relates to abdominal wall/rotation defects, not luminal narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incomplete stomach rotation affects gastric positioning, not jejunal luminal caliber.

questions.stem: During development the stomach undergoes a rotation that swings it into the left upper abdomen and creates a space directly posterior to it. What is this posterior space, and what movement creates it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lesser sac created by a 270-degree rotation of the midgut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peritoneal cavity created by lateral folding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Omental bursa created by a 90-degree clockwise rotation of the stomach

choices.label: D
choices.text: Omental bursa created by fusion of the ventral mesentery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retroperitoneal space created by mesenteric fusion

explanation.summary: The omental bursa forms behind the stomach as the stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise in the transverse plane, which moves it into the left upper quadrant and generates the omental bursa (lesser sac) posterior to it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 270-degree rotation applies to the midgut loop, not to the formation of the space behind the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lateral folding forms the whole peritoneal cavity, not the specific posterior gastric space.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ventral mesentery largely disappears; its fusion does not create the omental bursa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mesenteric fusion produces secondarily retroperitoneal organs, not the omental bursa.

questions.stem: The stomach develops an asymmetric shape with a long greater curvature and a short lesser curvature. Which developmental mechanism produces the greater curvature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster proliferation of the dorsal wall of the stomach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Faster proliferation of the ventral wall of the stomach

choices.label: C
choices.text: Traction from the persisting ventral mesentery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incomplete recanalization of the gastric lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fusion of the dorsal mesentery to the body wall

explanation.summary: Accelerated dorsal wall growth forms the greater curvature.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dorsal wall of the stomach grows faster than the ventral wall, forming the greater curvature; the shorter ventral wall becomes the lesser curvature.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The ventral wall grows more slowly and becomes the lesser (shorter) curvature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ventral mesentery persists only around the liver and does not create the greater curvature by traction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recanalization concerns luminal patency, not the external curvature shape.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dorsal mesentery fusion produces secondarily retroperitoneal positioning, not the greater curvature.

questions.stem: The midgut elongates into a loop that herniates into the umbilicus during week 6 and returns to the abdomen during week 10. Through what total angle does this loop rotate around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery before retracting?

explanation.summary: The midgut loop rotates a total of 270 degrees.
explanation.whyCorrect: The midgut loop rotates 270 degrees so its derivatives assume proper left/right positions when it returns to the abdomen in week 10.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 90 degrees is the rotation of the stomach, not the midgut loop.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 180 degrees is incomplete for correct final intestinal positioning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 45 degrees is far too little for proper gut positioning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A full 360 degrees would return the loop to its starting orientation, which does not occur.

questions.stem: A 10-week fetus has an abnormally formed cloaca. The cloaca is normally divided by a partition into a ventral and a dorsal compartment. What is this partition, and what are the two resulting compartments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Septum transversum dividing pleural and peritoneal cavities

choices.label: B
choices.text: Urorectal septum dividing a ventral urogenital sinus and a dorsal anorectal canal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Urorectal septum dividing a dorsal urogenital sinus and a ventral anorectal canal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tracheoesophageal septum dividing esophagus and trachea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dorsal mesentery dividing the peritoneal cavity

explanation.summary: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into a ventral urogenital sinus and a dorsal anorectal canal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cloaca is the widened caudal hindgut; the urorectal septum partitions it into a ventral urogenital sinus (bladder/urethra) and a dorsal anorectal canal (rectum/proximal anus).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The septum transversum forms the primitive diaphragm and liver scaffold, not cloacal division.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The orientation is reversed: the urogenital sinus is ventral and the anorectal canal is dorsal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The tracheoesophageal septum divides the foregut into trachea and esophagus, not the cloaca.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The dorsal mesentery anchors the gut; it does not divide the cloaca.

questions.stem: The anus develops from two sources, giving it two distinct blood and nerve supplies. The pectinate (dentate) line marks the junction between which two structures?

explanation.summary: The pectinate line is the junction of the hindgut-derived proximal anus and the anal-pit-derived distal anus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The internal proximal anus arises from the hindgut/cloaca and the external distal anus from the anal pit; they meet at the pectinate line, explaining the dual supply.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The foregut-midgut junction is in the duodenum, not at the anus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The midgut-hindgut junction is at the distal transverse colon, not the anus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cloaca is divided into the urogenital sinus and anorectal canal by the urorectal septum, but that is not the pectinate line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rectosigmoid junction is proximal to the anal canal and is not the pectinate line.

questions.stem: The hepatic diverticulum is an endodermal outgrowth from the ventral proximal duodenum. Its larger cranial portion grows along the septum transversum. What does this cranial portion become?

explanation.summary: The cranial hepatic diverticulum becomes the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cranial (larger) part of the hepatic diverticulum grows along the septum transversum to form the liver; the caudal part forms the gallbladder and cystic duct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gallbladder derives from the caudal part of the diverticulum, not the cranial part.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cystic duct also derives from the caudal part.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ventral pancreatic bud arises separately near the base of the diverticulum, not from its cranial part.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The common bile duct forms from the stalk connecting the diverticulum to the gut, not the cranial part.

questions.stem: The definitive pancreas forms from fusion of a dorsal and a ventral pancreatic bud arising from the duodenum. The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to which parts of the mature pancreas?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Uncinate process and the main pancreatic duct

explanation.summary: The ventral bud forms the uncinate process and the main pancreatic duct.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ventral pancreatic bud contributes the uncinate process (part of the head) and the main pancreatic duct; the dorsal bud forms the head, body, tail, and accessory duct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The head, body, and tail derive largely from the dorsal bud, not the ventral bud.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The accessory pancreatic duct comes from the dorsal bud, not the ventral bud.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The body and tail come from the dorsal bud.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No single bud forms the entire ductal system; the ducts derive from both buds combined.

questions.stem: Some abdominal organs begin development suspended intraperitoneally but later come to lie outside the peritoneal cavity when their dorsal mesentery fuses with the posterior body wall. Which set of organs best illustrates this 'secondarily retroperitoneal' fate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidneys, adrenal glands, and urinary bladder

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ascending colon, descending colon, duodenum, and pancreas

explanation.summary: Ascending/descending colon, duodenum, and pancreas are secondarily retroperitoneal.
explanation.whyCorrect: These organs start intraperitoneal, then their dorsal mesentery fuses with the posterior abdominal wall, leaving them behind the peritoneum (secondarily retroperitoneal).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stomach and spleen remain intraperitoneal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidneys, adrenals, and bladder are primarily (originally) retroperitoneal, arising outside the peritoneal cavity, not secondarily.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver and gallbladder remain intraperitoneal (the liver is invested by peritoneum).
whyWrongByChoice.E: The jejunum and ileum remain intraperitoneal, suspended by mesentery.

questions.stem: During development the two midline mesenteries have different fates. Which statement correctly describes the fate of the dorsal and ventral mesenteries?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The dorsal mesentery largely disappears; the ventral mesentery persists throughout the gut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both mesenteries persist along the entire gut tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: The dorsal mesentery largely persists; the ventral mesentery largely disappears except around the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ventral mesentery persists along the entire gut; the dorsal disappears at the stomach

explanation.summary: The dorsal mesentery persists; the ventral mesentery mostly disappears except at the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dorsal mesentery persists to anchor the gut and carry its vessels and nerves, while the ventral mesentery largely disappears, being retained only around the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the correct fates; the dorsal mesentery persists and the ventral largely disappears.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ventral mesentery does not persist along the entire gut; it mostly regresses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The dorsal mesentery does not disappear; it persists to suspend the gut.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ventral mesentery does not persist along the entire gut, and the dorsal mesentery persists rather than disappearing.

questions.stem: After lateral folding, the wall of the primitive gut tube (its muscular and connective-tissue layers, but not the epithelial lining) is formed predominantly from which tissue?

explanation.summary: The gut wall is formed from splanchnic mesoderm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The GI tract tube is built from endoderm (lining) plus splanchnic mesoderm, which forms most of the wall (muscle and connective tissue).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall on the opposite side of the coelom, not the gut wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining, not the muscular/connective wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surface ectoderm forms epidermis, not the gut wall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paraxial mesoderm (somites) forms axial skeleton and skeletal muscle, not the gut wall.

questions.stem: A key event in gut development is physiologic herniation of the midgut loop into the umbilical cord because the loop temporarily outgrows the abdominal cavity. During which developmental week does this herniation begin?

explanation.summary: Midgut herniation into the umbilicus begins in week 6.
explanation.whyCorrect: The midgut loop herniates into the umbilicus during week 6, rotates 270 degrees, and returns to the abdomen during week 10.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Week 3 is when the flat trilaminar embryonic disc forms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Week 4 is when lateral folding creates the body trunk and primitive gut tube.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Week 12 is after the loop has already returned.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Week 10 is when the midgut loop returns to the abdomen, not when it herniates.

questions.stem: During fetal development, one abdominal organ arises from a mesodermal condensation in the dorsal mesentery of the stomach, rotates with the stomach into the left upper quadrant, and is a major site of blood cell formation (hematopoiesis) at other developmental stages. Which pairing is correct regarding these developmental facts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The spleen forms in the dorsal mesentery; the liver is a major site of fetal hematopoiesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spleen forms from endoderm; the pancreas is the major site of fetal hematopoiesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The spleen forms in the ventral mesentery; the spleen is the sole site of fetal hematopoiesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The liver forms in the dorsal mesentery; the spleen is the major site of fetal hematopoiesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen is a foregut endodermal derivative; the gallbladder is a major site of fetal hematopoiesis

explanation.summary: The spleen is a mesodermal derivative of the dorsal mesentery; the liver is a major fetal hematopoietic organ.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen forms from a mesodermal condensation in the dorsal mesentery and rotates with the stomach to the left upper abdomen, while the liver serves as a major site of hematopoiesis during development.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The spleen is mesodermal, not endodermal, and the pancreas is not a major hematopoietic organ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spleen forms in the dorsal (not ventral) mesentery, and the liver is a major hematopoietic site during development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver is an endodermal (hepatic diverticulum) derivative, not a dorsal mesentery structure, and the liver (not spleen) is the major fetal hematopoietic organ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen is mesodermal, not a foregut endodermal derivative, and the gallbladder is not hematopoietic.

questions.stem: A neonate is found to have complete duodenal atresia. In terms of the recanalization process of the gut tube, which sequence best explains how a normally patent lumen is produced and where this fetus's development failed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lumen is always hollow; atresia results from failure of the tube to elongate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoderm proliferates and fills the lumen, then those cells are removed to reopen the tube; in atresia the cells are never removed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Splanchnic mesoderm fills the lumen, then is removed; in atresia the mesoderm never forms

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lumen forms by fusion of two solid rods; in atresia the rods fail to fuse

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lumen forms by apoptosis of the outer wall; in atresia the wall is retained

explanation.summary: Recanalization fills the lumen with proliferating endoderm then removes it; failure of removal causes atresia.
explanation.whyCorrect: During recanalization the endodermal epithelium proliferates and occludes the lumen, and those cells are then removed to restore a patent tube; complete failure of cell removal produces atresia (full obstruction).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lumen is not continuously hollow; it is transiently occluded by endodermal proliferation and then reopened, and atresia is a recanalization failure, not an elongation failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It is endoderm, not splanchnic mesoderm, that fills the lumen during recanalization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gut lumen is not formed by fusion of two solid rods.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recanalization removes luminal (inner) cells, not the outer wall, so this mechanism is incorrect.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy is brought to the emergency department because of forceful, projectile vomiting of undigested breast milk after every feeding for the past week. The vomitus is never green or yellow. He appears dehydrated and remains hungry immediately after emesis. On examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass is palpated in the right upper quadrant, and visible gastric peristalsis is noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Nonbilious projectile vomiting with a palpable olive-shaped mass in a first-born male infant is classic for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypertrophy of the pyloric smooth muscle produces gastric outlet obstruction. Because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla, vomiting is nonbilious and projectile; the hypertrophied pylorus is palpable as an olive in the RUQ with visible peristalsis, and the disorder classically affects first-born males aged 3-12 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Duodenal atresia presents within hours of birth with bilious vomiting, not at 5 weeks with nonbilious emesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Midgut volvulus causes bilious vomiting and a sick, unstable infant, not nonbilious vomiting with an olive mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hirschsprung disease presents with failure to pass meconium and distal obstruction, not projectile gastric vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Esophageal atresia presents at birth with drooling and inability to feed, not projectile vomiting weeks later.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A newborn with trisomy 21 develops bilious vomiting within the first hours of life. An abdominal radiograph shows two distinct gas-filled bubbles, one in the stomach and one in the proximal duodenum, with no distal bowel gas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting hours after birth with a double-bubble sign, especially in an infant with Down syndrome, indicates duodenal atresia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Duodenal atresia results from failed recanalization of the duodenum. Gas distends the stomach and proximal duodenum proximal to the atretic segment, producing the double-bubble sign, and roughly one third of affected infants have Down syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyloric stenosis causes nonbilious vomiting at 3-12 weeks and shows a single gastric bubble, not a double bubble.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meckel's diverticulum classically causes painless lower GI bleeding in older infants, not neonatal proximal obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meconium ileus causes distal small-bowel obstruction with failure to pass meconium, not a proximal double bubble.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imperforate anus is diagnosed on physical exam by an absent anal opening, not by a double-bubble sign.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A previously healthy, thriving 3-week-old infant suddenly develops bilious (green) vomiting and becomes irritable and lethargic over a few hours. The abdomen is initially soft but the infant appears increasingly unstable. Which of the following diagnoses is the most urgent consideration?

explanation.summary: Sudden bilious vomiting in a previously well infant is midgut volvulus until proven otherwise, a surgical emergency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malrotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base; once feeding challenges intestinal function, the bowel can twist (volvulus), occluding the superior mesenteric vessels and threatening necrosis of the entire small intestine. Bilious vomiting in an infant is an emergency until proven otherwise.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reflux produces nonbilious spit-up in a comfortable infant and is not a surgical emergency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyloric stenosis causes nonbilious projectile vomiting, not the bilious emesis seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meckel's diverticulum typically causes painless bleeding, not acute bilious vomiting with instability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hirschsprung disease presents with failure to pass meconium and constipation, not acute bilious vomiting in a thriving infant.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A term newborn fails to pass meconium in the first 48 hours of life and develops abdominal distension. A suction rectal biopsy of the distal rectum demonstrates an absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Failure to pass meconium with aganglionosis on rectal biopsy defines Hirschsprung disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hirschsprung disease results from failed craniocaudal migration of neural crest cells, leaving the distal bowel without ganglion cells. The aganglionic segment is permanently contracted, causing functional obstruction and delayed meconium passage; rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells is diagnostic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Duodenal stenosis causes proximal obstruction with bilious vomiting, not distal aganglionosis or delayed meconium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Meconium ileus causes distal obstruction but biopsy shows normal ganglion cells; the problem is inspissated meconium, usually with cystic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Annular pancreas encircles the duodenum causing proximal obstruction, unrelated to rectal ganglion cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biliary atresia presents with jaundice and acholic stools weeks later, not neonatal aganglionosis.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: Shortly after birth, a newborn has excessive drooling, coughing, and choking with attempts to feed, and becomes cyanotic. Nursing staff are unable to advance a nasogastric tube into the stomach; a radiograph shows the tube coiled in the upper esophageal pouch. The mother's pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Drooling, feeding intolerance, and a nasogastric tube coiling in a blind upper pouch after a polyhydramnios pregnancy indicate esophageal atresia, most commonly with a distal TEF.
explanation.whyCorrect: Esophageal atresia results from failed recanalization of the foregut tube; the esophagus ends blindly, so an NG tube coils in the upper pouch and saliva pools, causing drooling and choking. Impaired fetal swallowing produces polyhydramnios. The most common form (Gross type C, ~86%) includes a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyloric stenosis presents at 3-12 weeks with projectile vomiting, not neonatal drooling or an obstructed NG tube.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and distal obstruction, not inability to pass an NG tube into the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meconium ileus causes distal bowel obstruction, not an obstructed esophagus or drooling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Malrotation causes bilious vomiting from midgut obstruction, not a blind esophageal pouch.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A 4-week-old boy with a 10-day history of projectile nonbilious vomiting is dehydrated. Serum electrolytes are obtained. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most characteristic of his condition?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically causes a hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Persistent vomiting of gastric contents loses hydrochloric acid and potassium, producing hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion drives renal sodium (and thus bicarbonate) retention, and to conserve sodium the kidney secretes hydrogen ions, causing paradoxically acidic urine despite systemic alkalosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A hyperkalemic, hyperchloremic acidosis is the opposite of the loss of acid and potassium seen with gastric vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An anion-gap acidosis with hyperlactatemia suggests ischemia (e.g., volvulus), not uncomplicated pyloric stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is a metabolic alkalosis, not a respiratory process, and sodium is typically low from volume loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal anion-gap acidosis with hyperkalemia does not match the alkalosis produced by loss of gastric acid.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with painless passage of dark red blood per rectum. He is hemodynamically stable and has no abdominal pain. Surgical exploration reveals a true diverticulum arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum. From which embryologic structure did this lesion most likely arise?

explanation.summary: A true ileal diverticulum causing painless bleeding is a Meckel's diverticulum from a persistent vitelline duct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Meckel's diverticulum arises from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, leaving a true diverticulum containing all bowel wall layers on the antimesenteric ileum. Ectopic gastric mucosa within it secretes acid, ulcerating adjacent ileum and causing painless lower GI bleeding, the leading cause in young children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A persistent urachus connects the bladder to the umbilicus and causes urinary drainage, not ileal bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed foregut recanalization produces esophageal or duodenal atresia, not an ileal diverticulum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease, not a Meckel's diverticulum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An in-utero vascular accident is the proposed mechanism of jejunoileal atresia, not of a true diverticulum.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A newborn develops abdominal distension and fails to pass meconium in the first 48 hours. Contrast enema shows a microcolon with inspissated meconium pellets obstructing the terminal ileum, and there is no evidence of aganglionosis. Which underlying disease is most strongly associated with this presentation?

explanation.summary: Meconium ileus with thick inspissated meconium obstructing the ileum is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In meconium ileus, abnormally thick, inspissated meconium obstructs the distal small bowel. About 85% of cases are associated with cystic fibrosis, and meconium ileus may be its initial presentation. Non-operative management (contrast enema) is often successful.

whyWrongByChoice.A: VACTERL is associated with esophageal atresia/TEF and imperforate anus, not with inspissated meconium ileus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Down syndrome is associated with duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease, not classically meconium ileus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Turner syndrome is not the classic association of meconium ileus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 18 is not the disease strongly linked to meconium ileus.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A 5-week-old infant presents with nonbilious projectile vomiting and a suspected palpable epigastric mass. Which of the following imaging studies is the confirmatory test of choice for the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Ultrasound is the confirmatory test of choice for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ultrasound directly visualizes the hypertrophied pylorus, showing increased pyloric muscle thickness, length, and diameter (hypertrophic values roughly 22.5 mm length, 14 mm diameter, 6 mm muscle thickness versus normal ~12 mm length and 7 mm diameter). It is non-invasive and avoids radiation, making it the confirmatory test of choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CT delivers unnecessary radiation and is not used to confirm pyloric stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Barium enema evaluates the colon (e.g., Hirschsprung), not the pylorus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Meckel scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum, not pyloric hypertrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An upper GI series is used for suspected malrotation; ultrasound is preferred to confirm pyloric stenosis.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the embryologic tissue contributions to the gastrointestinal tract wall. The intrinsic innervation (enteric ganglia) of the gut is derived from which of the following?

explanation.summary: The innervation of the GI tract is derived from neural crest cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: During development, endoderm forms the lining epithelium and glands, mesoderm forms the smooth muscle and connective tissue, and neural crest cells (originating from the ectoderm) migrate craniocaudally to form the enteric ganglia. Failure of this migration causes Hirschsprung disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endoderm gives rise to the lining epithelium and glands, not the neuronal innervation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splanchnic mesoderm forms the smooth muscle and connective tissue of the gut wall, not the ganglia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The notochord induces neural tube formation but does not form gut innervation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites (bone and skeletal muscle), not enteric ganglia.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A newborn has bilious vomiting and feeding intolerance. Imaging shows a ring of tissue encircling and narrowing the second part of the duodenum. This anomaly results from failure of which embryologic process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of the ventral pancreatic bud to rotate normally, encircling the duodenum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the gut wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the midgut to complete counterclockwise rotation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of the foregut to separate from the trachea

explanation.summary: A ring of pancreatic tissue encircling the duodenum is an annular pancreas from abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pancreas develops from ventral and dorsal buds. Normally the ventral bud rotates posteriorly to fuse with the dorsal bud. If the ventral bud fails to rotate correctly, it encircles the second part of the duodenum as a ring of pancreatic tissue (annular pancreas), causing duodenal obstruction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Failure of vitelline duct obliteration produces Meckel's diverticulum, not a pancreatic ring around the duodenum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease of the colon, not annular pancreas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incomplete midgut rotation causes malrotation with a short mesentery, not a ring of pancreatic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failed foregut separation from the trachea causes tracheoesophageal fistula, not an annular pancreas.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A newborn is diagnosed with esophageal atresia and a distal tracheoesophageal fistula. The neonatology team screens for additional anomalies. This combination is most commonly associated with which of the following groupings of congenital defects?

explanation.summary: Esophageal atresia and TEF are most commonly associated with the VACTERL association.
explanation.whyCorrect: VACTERL denotes Vertebral, Anal (imperforate anus), Cardiac, Tracheo-Esophageal, Renal, and Limb anomalies. Esophageal atresia/TEF and imperforate anus are core components, so any infant with EA/TEF should be screened for the other VACTERL defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CHARGE syndrome is associated with coloboma and choanal atresia; EA/TEF is classically linked to VACTERL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beckwith-Wiedemann features macrosomia, macroglossia, and omphalocele, not the EA/TEF cluster.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DiGeorge syndrome involves thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia and conotruncal cardiac defects, not the defining EA/TEF association.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potter sequence results from oligohydramnios and renal agenesis, unrelated to esophageal atresia.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: An infant with prolonged vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction is found to have alkalotic serum but urine that is paradoxically acidic. Which renal mechanism best explains the paradoxical aciduria in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased renal bicarbonate excretion in response to alkalosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Volume depletion driving sodium reabsorption at the expense of hydrogen ion secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Distal renal tubular acidosis impairing hydrogen ion secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excess renal ammonia production from hepatic dysfunction

explanation.summary: Volume depletion forces avid renal sodium reabsorption; hydrogen ions are secreted to accompany it, acidifying the urine despite systemic alkalosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ongoing vomiting causes volume depletion and hypokalemia. The kidney prioritizes sodium and volume conservation, activating aldosterone; in the collecting duct sodium is reabsorbed in exchange for secretion of hydrogen (and potassium) ions. This continued acid loss in the urine, alongside worsening hypokalemia, produces paradoxically acidic urine even though the plasma is alkalotic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: If the kidney simply excreted bicarbonate, the urine would be alkaline and the alkalosis would self-correct; that is not what happens here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is secondary, volume-driven aldosterone activation, not a primary aldosterone-secreting tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Distal RTA causes a metabolic acidosis, not the metabolic alkalosis with aciduria described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatic dysfunction and ammonia handling do not explain the paradoxical aciduria of gastric fluid loss.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A newborn has bilious vomiting and distension. At laparotomy, a segment of small bowel ends blindly with a corresponding gap in the mesentery, and the distal bowel is collapsed. The pathophysiology of this jejunoileal atresia is best explained by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of the foregut tube to recanalize

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: An in-utero mesenteric vascular accident with resorption of ischemic bowel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Encirclement of the bowel by ectopic pancreatic tissue

explanation.summary: Jejunoileal atresia is thought to result from an in-utero mesenteric vascular accident.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike duodenal atresia (a recanalization defect), jejunoileal atresia is attributed to an intrauterine vascular accident that compromises a segment of bowel; the ischemic segment is resorbed, leaving a blind-ending proximal bowel, a mesenteric gap, and collapsed distal bowel. Atresia can be solitary or multiple.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failed foregut recanalization explains esophageal and duodenal atresia, not mid-small-bowel atresia with a mesenteric defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease, not a blind-ending atretic small bowel.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A persistent vitelline duct produces Meckel's diverticulum, not jejunoileal atresia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ectopic pancreatic tissue encircling bowel describes annular pancreas at the duodenum, not jejunoileal atresia.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
questions.stem: A pediatrician is teaching about the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, present in roughly 2% of the population and usually asymptomatic. Which of the following statements about this lesion is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a false (pulsion) diverticulum containing only mucosa and submucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: It most commonly arises from the sigmoid colon

choices.label: C
choices.text: It results from failed neural crest migration

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is diagnosed definitively by abdominal ultrasound of the pylorus

choices.label: E
choices.text: When symptomatic, it commonly bleeds due to acid secreted by ectopic gastric mucosa

explanation.summary: A Meckel's diverticulum, present in about 2% of people, bleeds when ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid that ulcerates adjacent ileum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most Meckel's diverticula are asymptomatic (~98%). When symptomatic, ectopic gastric (or pancreatic) mucosa secretes acid that ulcerates the neighboring ileal mucosa, producing painless lower GI bleeding, the leading cause in young children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Meckel's is a true diverticulum containing all layers of the bowel wall, not a false diverticulum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It arises from the antimesenteric ileum, not the sigmoid colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease; Meckel's is from a persistent vitelline duct.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It is detected with a technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan, not pyloric ultrasound.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the GI Tract
